title: Cold Call
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles makes the case for cold calling as the single most valuable change a teacher can make to checking for understanding. He stages a fictional post-observation feedback conversation in which every answer in the lesson came from the same seven volunteers. By splitting the books into volunteers and non-volunteers, the teacher discovers that the rest of the class was well below the success criteria, something volunteer answers had hidden. The argument is that volunteers give a false picture of whole-class understanding, whereas random questioning samples everyone and reveals misconceptions in time to reteach. He then extrapolates the effect, with the teacher's own estimates, to half a grade across Years 10 and 11 and a full grade across Years 7 to 11. The call is close between pedagogy and coaching, but the questioning technique drives the argument.
points: Volunteers self-select, so questions answered only by them tell a teacher nothing reliable about the other 29 students.
Comparing books from the seven volunteers against everyone else makes the sampling gap visible: nearly all volunteers met the criteria while few others did.
Random questioning would have exposed the gap during the lesson, prompting a reteach with a new example and turn and talk.
Salles pre-empts the Teach Like a Champion backlash by arguing technique and relationships are not in conflict, and that Cold Call will change the lives of students.
quotes: Not so fast. Cold Call will change your life, and the lives of your students.
The one thing I spotted which will add most to your students’ progress is Cold Call. You asked 6 questions while I was there, and they were all answered by volunteers.
But they were all volunteers, who self selected. I only noticed the same 7 students raising their hands. Does that suggest only 7 students understood?
6 of the 7 volunteers met all three of my criteria. The rest of the class seem to average around 1 or 2, and only 2 students from this group managed to do all 3.

Now, imagine all your questions were to random students. If you asked 6 questions, at least 4 of those are likely to have gone to non-volunteers. You would probably have seen that most of the class hadn’t fully understood. What would you have done then?

I would have spotted that I needed to write about structure with another example, probably jointly constructing it with students using turn and talk. And I would also have asked them to show me what words proved that a one-word quote was being analysed.
Well, I reckoned half a grade in year 10 and 11, so I guess Key Stage 3 would be another half a grade. So, a full grade higher. That would be 30X!
